Moody's 25 Apr. 1862 Civil War letter ('a phoney scrape and also a serious one, too', CERT-2200-105, shown to be rural Georgia phonetic 'funny scrape'); dates A. adj. to 29 June 1893 Chicago Daily Tribune ('"phony" bookmakers', CERT-2200-110; figurative human insincerity 1900 G. Ade 'Phoney Acting', CERT-2200-003); dates B. noun to 1902 C. L. (OED1 1895, modified Dec. 2025; < Irish fáinne 'ring'): dates 'fawney rig' / 'fawney' to 1781 George Parker View of Society & Manners II.166-167 (CERT-2200-305) and 'fawney-dropping' to Nov. 1827 Morning Chronicle (cf. 12 July 1827 Old Bailey spoken 'fawneys', CERT-2200-310).

wordorigins_and_specialist_literature.baselines: Peter Tamony ('The Origin of "Phoney"', American Speech 12.2 [Apr. 1937]: 108-110) established the structural derivation from Anglo-Irish cant fawney ('gilt-brass ring') via street jewelry peddlers. Paul S. Cohen (Transactions of the Philological Society 109.1 [2011]: 59-72) audited the fawney -> phoney phonological pathway and the 1862 Moody letter. Dave Wilton (Wordorigins.org, 10 Feb. 2022) pushed print attestations ahead of OED3's June 1893 baseline to the 4 April 1890 Detroit Plaindealer wire-marriage pun ('quite a \'phoney\' joke', CERT-2200-108) and the unambiguous 7 May 1892 Washington Evening Star baseball report ('a little on the phony order', CERT-2200-109).

greens_dictionary_of_slang_and_hdas.baselines: Green's Dictionary of Slang dates phoney, adj. to 17 Nov. 1894 Decatur Daily Review ('phony ticket'), phoney, n.1 to 1902 Cullen (imitation diamond sense 1908), fawney man ('bogus jewelry peddler') to 1899 Josiah Flynt Tramping with Tramps 280, and phony men to 30 June 1900 National Police Gazette (CERT-2200-216). Case 2200 antedates GDoS 'fawny men' to Feb. 1894 Century Magazine (CERT-2200-206, 5 yrs, 7 mos earlier), GDoS 'phony men' to 15 Aug. 1894 Maysville Evening Bulletin ('"Phoney" Jewelry Man', CERT-2200-114, 5 yrs, 10 mos earlier), and OED3/GDoS nominal phoney, n. (1902) to 20 July 1895 St. Louis Post-Dispatch ('"phonies"', CERT-2200-116, 6 yrs, 8 mos earlier; 21 yrs, 4 mos earlier than OED3's 1916 plural), 9 Apr. 1896 Daily Racing Form ('a \'phony\'' = bogus $5 coin, CERT-2200-208), and 4 May 1897 St. Louis Post-Dispatch ('a "phony"' = fake diamond stud, CERT-2200-210).

citations.attested_form: FAIN & Fainne, a ring; rectius ain', ainne a circle, a ring
citations.short_gloss: Earliest printed Irish-English dictionary entry for Irish fainne ('a ring; a circle, a ring') in Bishop John O'Brien's Paris Focaloir (1768), thirteen years before Parker's 1781 'Fawney Rig'
citations.source_publication: John O'Brien, Focaloir Gaoidhilge-Sax-Bhearla, or an Irish-English Dictionary (Paris: Printed by Nicolas-Francis Valleyre, for the Author, 1768 [M. DCC. LXVIII])
citations.page_and_column: Title leaf (n8, 'M. DCC. LXVIII'), p. 228, col. 1 ('FAIN & Fainne, a ring', leaf n294) & col. 2 ('FAINNE, ignorance', leaf n294)
citations.verbatim_quote: FAIN & Fainne, a ring; rectius ain', ainne a circle, a ring. vid. remarks on A. | [col. 2:] FAINNE, ignorance.
citations.linguistic_note: Ultimate Celtic donor lemma: Old and Middle Irish ainne ('finger-ring', diminutive/derivative of ain 'ring, circle'; eDIL dil.ie/1351 & dil.ie/21121) acquired prothetic f- via regular lenition reanalysis after the masculine genitive/dative article and prepositions, yielding Classical and Modern Irish fainne [fa:n'e], realized in Munster and southern Irish with strong labial-velar rounding before tense palatalized nasal -nn- as [fo:n'e] — the exact phonetic model for 18th-century St Giles Rookery / Anglo-Irish cant fawney [fo:ni] ('finger-ring').
citations.analysis_notes: Scan-verified on the 1768 Paris first edition (title page M. DCC. LXVIII, leaf n8; p. 228, leaf n294). Bishop John O'Brien of Cloyne and Ross (County Cork, Munster) records both the spoken vernacular form 'Fainne, a ring' with its etymological cross-reference to historical vowel-initial 'ainne, a circle, a ring' (col. 1) and the distinct short-vowel abstract noun 'FAINNE, ignorance' (< fann 'weak', col. 2) on the very same page. Published thirteen years before George Parker's 1781 London cant attestation ('The FAWNEY RIG' / 'Fawney'), O'Brien's Munster lexicon anchors the donor form chronologically, semantically, and dialectally.

citations.attested_form: The FAWNEY RIG / THE Fawney / going on the Fawney
citations.short_gloss: Earliest known English attestation of 'The FAWNEY RIG' and 'Fawney' in George Parker's A View of Society and Manners, Vol. II (1781), already documenting wholesale fake-ring supply shops
citations.source_publication: George Parker, A View of Society and Manners in High and Low Life, Vol. II (London: Printed for the Author, 1781 [M,DCC,LXXXI])
citations.source_archive: Internet Archive (Eighteenth Century Collections Online / British Library)
citations.page_and_column: Vol. II Title Page (leaf n0, 'M,DCC,LXXXI') & pp. 166-167 (leaves n173-n174)
citations.verbatim_quote: [p. 166:] The FAWNEY RIG. A RING-DROPPER; a fellow who has gotten a woman's pocket, with a pair of scissars, some thread, a thimble, and a housewife with a ring in it, which he drops for some credulous person to pick up. | [p. 167:] THE Fawney says, "I dare say some poor woman has lost her pocket. Good gracious! here's a ring, and her wedding-ring too, for here's a poesy;" then reads, "Love me and leave me not," or some such thing. ... Queer as this rig may appear, there is a large shop in London where these kind of rings are sold, for the purpose of going on the Fawney.
citations.linguistic_note: Foundational Anglo-Irish cant borrowing and typographic control: uppercase roman F in 'The FAWNEY RIG' (p. 166) and crossbarred italic F in 'Fawney' (p. 167, twice) stand in unmistakable visual contrast to uncrossed medial long-s in 'scissars', 'some', 'person', 'says', 'say', 'lost', 'shop', 'these', 'sold', and 'purpose', ruling out any 18th-century long-s confusion with 'Sawney'. Notice too that in Parker (1781) 'THE Fawney' also denotes the ring-dropper himself by metonymy, and the ring already bears a pre-engraved sentimental posy ('Love me and leave me not') bought at a wholesale London swag shop ('worth about sixpence... intrinsic value of it is not a halfpenny')—the identical business model attested 121 years later in Fort Wayne's 1902 '"phoney" ring peddler' selling $1-a-dozen brass rings engraved 'Joe to Sue' (CERT-2200-219).
citations.analysis_notes: Re-minted cleanly in the 2200-3XX series with fresh 1800px ECCO scans of Vol. II title leaf n0 ('LONDON: PRINTED FOR THE AUTHOR, M,DCC,LXXXI') and pp. 166-167 (leaves n173-n174). Establishes OED3's 1781 baseline for fawney rig and confirms that wholesale manufacture of pre-inscribed gilt-brass confidence rings accompanied the word from its very first appearance in English print.
